lessons.title: Welcome to BuildAndDo
lessons.summary: Learn the Observe → Understand → Act → Verify loop and read workspace state without mistaking a plan for a result.
lessons.prerequisites: None — start here.

outcomes: Identify the four parts of the work loop.
Distinguish missing data from a failed data request.
lesson.why: A shared workspace is useful only when people can tell an observation, a proposal and a verified result apart. This habit prevents an attractive dashboard from becoming a substitute for evidence.
preparation: Open BuildAndDo; sign in only when saving an exercise.
Use a test workspace you are allowed to change.

sections.heading: Understand the idea
paragraphs: Observe means record what a source actually returned. Understand means explain what that observation might mean and keep uncertainty visible. Act means perform an approved, bounded step. Verify means inspect whether its stated outcome happened.

Counts summarize saved records. An empty list can be valid, while an unavailable notice means the application cannot currently tell you what is stored. Refreshing a page does not authorize a mission or deploy a release.

sections.heading: Try it in BuildAndDo
steps: Open Overview and identify the active workspace.
Visit Signals and Evidence Ledger; find the displayed source and timestamp, or the explicit empty state.
Open Missions and compare a proposed item with a finished outcome if either exists.
Write down one observation and one question you still cannot answer.

sections.heading: Worked example — illustrative data
paragraphs: Illustration: a reminder mission is proposed after five missed appointments. The proposal is not five messages sent. Keep the observation, approval, attempt and delivery receipt as separate records.

exercise.prompt: Describe one small business problem using the four stages. Save real records only if you have permission.
checklist: Name the source of the observation.
Identify the approval needed before acting.
Specify an observable result.

check.question: A mission has been saved as proposed. What can you conclude?
choices: Its business outcome is verified.
A proposal was recorded; execution and outcome remain unproven.
The related service is installed.
check.explanation: A saved proposal proves that the plan exists. Later actions and evidence are separate observations.

lessons.legacy_summary: The Observe → Understand → Act → Verify loop, and how your workspace is organized.

lessons.title: Selecting and verifying a domain
lessons.summary: Separate a discovered domain, a selected target and permission to operate on it.
lessons.prerequisites: Read earlier lessons in this path; use an authorized test workspace for exercises.

outcomes: Describe selected versus verified domain state.
Record what ownership evidence is still missing.
lesson.why: A hostname is an address, not a grant of authority. Keeping ownership and verification separate helps you avoid running an otherwise reasonable task against the wrong organization.
preparation: Have a domain you control or use an explicitly labelled example.
Do not enter DNS credentials or verification secrets in notes.

sections.heading: Understand the idea
paragraphs: Discovery produces a candidate. Selection chooses a candidate for a workspace. Verification needs an observed result from the authorized ownership-check process; do not infer it from a matching name.

A domain may serve different staging and production sites. Permission for a test environment does not automatically cover production. The workspace record should describe which environment and action are intended.

sections.heading: Try it in BuildAndDo
steps: Inspect the workspace identity and any selected domain in Settings.
Compare the hostname with the organization and environment you intend to use.
Record the ownership check you have actually observed, or state that verification is pending.
Scope the next mission to the permitted environment and stop if authority is unclear.

sections.heading: Worked example — illustrative data
paragraphs: Illustration: selecting example.com for a learning exercise does not establish ownership of that reserved example domain. A note saying “example only, no live action” keeps the exercise honest.

exercise.prompt: Write a domain-verification note with target, environment, authority source and missing evidence.
checklist: Spell the target hostname exactly.
Separate observed ownership from a pending check.
Exclude credentials and secret values.

check.question: Does selecting a domain authorize changes to its DNS?
choices: Yes, if the domain appears in search.
Yes, after adding it to a workspace.
No; ownership and the specific change authority must be established.
check.explanation: Selection is an organizational choice. Ownership verification and permission for the intended change are separate.

lessons.legacy_summary: How domain discovery works, what 'selected' vs 'verified' means, and why a found domain is not an authorized domain.

lessons.title: Reading the Signals feed
lessons.summary: Read observations, confidence and timestamps before turning a signal into work.
lessons.prerequisites: Read earlier lessons in this path; use an authorized test workspace for exercises.

outcomes: Separate a source fact from an interpretation.
Identify one useful follow-up check.
lesson.why: Signals compete for attention. Preserving source and freshness lets a team act on the strongest observation rather than the most dramatic wording.
preparation: Open Signals in an authorized workspace.
If there are no records, use the illustrative example without inventing a live event.

sections.heading: Understand the idea
paragraphs: A fact is an observation attributed to a source at a time. An inference explains that observation and can be wrong. Confidence describes uncertainty; it does not make an inference a fact.
Old signals can remain useful history but should not be presented as current system health. A missing timestamp or inaccessible source is a reason to gather more evidence before escalating.

sections.heading: Try it in BuildAndDo
steps: Choose one signal and read its source, timestamp and displayed confidence.
Restate only what the source observed in one sentence.
Write a separate possible explanation and an alternative explanation.
Choose a small check that distinguishes those explanations before proposing a mission.

sections.heading: Worked example — illustrative data
paragraphs: Illustration: “three failed requests in ten minutes” is an observation. “The new release is broken” is a hypothesis; a service outage or client network failure could explain the same count.

exercise.prompt: Prepare a short signal assessment with one fact, two hypotheses and a next check.
checklist: Keep the source and observation time.
Use uncertainty language for explanations.
Define what new evidence would change your conclusion.

check.question: Which statement is an inference?
choices: The release caused the error spike.
The log contains three failed requests.
The observation was recorded at 09:00 UTC.
check.explanation: Causation requires additional evidence. A count or timestamp can be a direct observation when its source is recorded.

lessons.legacy_summary: Telling facts, inferences, and user-provided information apart, and what confidence means.

lessons.title: Proposing and approving a mission
lessons.summary: Build a bounded mission plan with explicit authorization, success criteria and review.
lessons.prerequisites: Read earlier lessons in this path; use an authorized test workspace for exercises.

outcomes: Save a useful mission draft.
Explain why approval is distinct from starting work.
lesson.why: A clear proposal makes the approver’s decision reviewable. The person authorizing work should know its scope, limits and recovery plan before anyone records work started.
preparation: Read a real signal or choose an illustrative business problem.
Identify an authorized approver; use demo mode for read-only exploration.

sections.heading: Understand the idea
paragraphs: A mission plan connects a beneficiary and purpose with a bounded change. Include the current baseline, measurable target, allowed systems, risk, authorization and rollback.

BuildAndDo records planning, approval, work and review. An approved status does not start a private agent. Revising approved scope requires a new approval rather than quietly carrying old permission forward.

sections.heading: Try it in BuildAndDo
steps: Open Missions and create a proposed mission.
Describe the purpose, beneficiary and exactly what is inside the scope.
Add a baseline, target, recovery plan and four TEVV methods.
Save the proposal and inspect it before the authorized approval action.

sections.heading: Worked example — illustrative data
paragraphs: Illustration: “Test one reminder template with consenting staff in the test workspace; compare delivery receipts; send no customer messages” is a bounded experiment. “Improve communications” is not.

exercise.prompt: Draft a mission that can be completed and checked in one short session.
checklist: State one measurable success criterion.
Name an explicit out-of-scope action.
Describe what happens if the check fails.

check.question: What should happen after materially changing an approved scope?
choices: Keep the old approval automatically.
Return the plan for approval of the new scope.
Mark the mission verified.
check.explanation: The new scope changes what was authorized. The saved approval must describe the work actually being performed.

lessons.legacy_summary: How a bounded mission is scoped, what you approve before anything runs, and how to review the plan.

lessons.title: Inspecting evidence and replay
lessons.summary: Use source-backed observations to review a mission without turning a receipt into a claim it cannot support.
lessons.prerequisites: Read earlier lessons in this path; use an authorized test workspace for exercises.

outcomes: Connect evidence to the correct mission and workspace.
Separate a recorded review from independent verification.
lesson.why: A receipt is valuable because someone else can inspect what happened. Evidence without a source or a clear connection to the claim makes reviews impossible to reproduce.
preparation: Use an existing test mission or inspect the example.
Remove customer information from learning artifacts.

sections.heading: Understand the idea
paragraphs: An evidence entry needs enough content, source and context to explain the observation. A mission review must reference readable evidence from the same mission and workspace.
A screenshot may prove that a screen displayed a value, but it does not prove that a backend transaction committed. A reviewer’s assertion is not a signed credential or an external certification.

sections.heading: Try it in BuildAndDo
steps: Open Evidence Ledger and inspect one entry’s content and source.
Check the associated mission and workspace.
Compare the observation with one stated acceptance criterion.
Record a limitation or a missing check before choosing a mission outcome.

sections.heading: Worked example — illustrative data
paragraphs: Illustration: a “saved” toast is UI evidence. A returned record ID followed by a successful authorized read adds persistence evidence. Neither proves a notification reached an external recipient.

exercise.prompt: Write an evidence note explaining what a receipt proves and what it does not.
checklist: Identify the exact claim being assessed.
Keep a readable source reference.
Record one practical limitation.

check.question: Can a UI success message alone prove external delivery?
choices: Yes, because it is visible.
Yes, if a reviewer clicks complete.
No; external delivery requires its own observable receipt.
check.explanation: Evidence should match the claim. UI state and external delivery are different events.

lessons.legacy_summary: How to review what BuildAndDo observed, decided, attempted, and verified — and what to do when a mission needs attention.

lessons.title: Connecting a self-hosted service
lessons.summary: Read service connection state and prepare a useful operations handoff.
lessons.prerequisites: Read earlier lessons in this path; use an authorized test workspace for exercises.

outcomes: Explain requested, connected and healthy states.
Prepare a connection acceptance check.
lesson.why: A connection request is useful coordination, but confusing it with a running integration can hide the absence of real data.
preparation: Identify a service and an operator authorized to configure it.
Keep host credentials in the private environment.

sections.heading: Understand the idea
paragraphs: Operations records the services relevant to the workspace. A pending connection indicates requested work; it does not install software or configure a host.

Connection and health are separate claims. An endpoint may accept authentication but fail its useful operation. Prefer a timestamped, minimal read or test receipt to a label with no backing observation.

sections.heading: Try it in BuildAndDo
steps: Open Operations and inspect the service catalogue and any saved state.
Identify the operator who owns the actual private setup.
Write the smallest authorized acceptance check and its expected response.
Keep the state pending until the operator returns the check’s result.

sections.heading: Worked example — illustrative data
paragraphs: Illustration: a CRM connection is requested. A later authorized list request returns one synthetic test contact and a timestamp. That receipt supports the read path, not every CRM feature.

exercise.prompt: Prepare an operations note for one service connection without including a secret.
checklist: Name the operator and intended environment.
Describe a minimal non-production check.
Separate configuration completion from useful-operation health.

check.question: A service shows Pending. What is established?
choices: A connection has been requested or is awaiting completion.
The service is healthy.
All its data has synchronized.
check.explanation: Pending is coordination state. Health and synchronization need later observations.

lessons.legacy_summary: What the Operations area means, the planned self-hosted stack, and how connection status works.

lessons.title: Define a measurable business objective
lessons.summary: Turn a broad ambition into an ERP objective with a useful success measure and review date.
lessons.prerequisites: Read earlier lessons in this path; use an authorized test workspace for exercises.

outcomes: Describe a baseline, target and observation period.
Save and edit an ERP objective.
lesson.why: A measurable objective helps people decide which tasks matter and when the work is sufficient. The measure should reflect a business result rather than the number of buttons clicked.
preparation: Choose one process you understand.
Use an observed baseline or explicitly mark it as unknown.

sections.heading: Understand the idea
paragraphs: An objective describes a desired result. A task describes an action that may help produce it. Keep them separate so task completion does not automatically imply business success.
A useful success measure identifies the quantity, population, period and source. If you have no baseline, the first task should gather it; inventing a number makes later evaluation meaningless.

sections.heading: Try it in BuildAndDo
steps: Open ERP, choose Objectives and add an objective.
Write a short result-oriented title and a description of the affected process.
Enter a success measure with baseline, target, period and source.
Set a review due date, save, then reopen the record to confirm the stored fields.

sections.heading: Worked example — illustrative data
paragraphs: Illustration: “Reduce test appointment no-shows from 5 of 40 to at most 3 of 40 over the next four weeks, using the booking export.” These numbers are educational examples, not live results.

exercise.prompt: Create or sketch one objective whose result a second person could assess.
checklist: Separate the intended result from an action.
Identify a source for the measure.
Keep unknown baseline values explicitly unknown.

check.question: Which is the stronger success measure?
choices: Make the process better.
Use the dashboard every day.
Reduce median response time from an observed baseline to a named target over a defined period.
check.explanation: The last measure defines an assessable outcome. Activity alone does not establish improvement.

lessons.title: Break an objective into linked tasks
lessons.summary: Create small ERP tasks that remain connected to the objective they support.
lessons.prerequisites: Read earlier lessons in this path; use an authorized test workspace for exercises.

outcomes: Save a task with a clear completion condition.
Link it to the correct workspace objective and contact.
lesson.why: A task list becomes easier to prioritize when each action has a visible purpose. Linking a task to an objective preserves that context during handoffs.
preparation: Have one saved objective.
Add a test contact only if you have permission to store the information.

sections.heading: Understand the idea
paragraphs: A good task names an action and the observable artifact it should produce. “Investigate” needs a boundary, such as producing a one-page comparison of two options.
A linked contact is a point of coordination, not an account permission or an assignment notification. The server requires related records to be readable in the same workspace.

sections.heading: Try it in BuildAndDo
steps: Open ERP Tasks and add a task.
Describe the action and expected result in the task details.
Choose the saved objective and an optional point of contact.
Save, reopen and confirm that the links and details survived the write.

sections.heading: Worked example — illustrative data
paragraphs: Illustration: objective “Reduce no-shows”; task “Compare two reminder templates using ten synthetic bookings”; contact “Test coordinator.” The task produces a comparison, not an automatic customer campaign.

exercise.prompt: Break one objective into three tasks with different observable outputs.
checklist: Link each task to the objective.
Make each output reviewable.
Keep customer outreach outside the exercise unless separately authorized.

check.question: Does choosing a contact grant that person workspace access?
choices: Yes, contacts are workspace members.
No; contact records and account permissions are separate.
Only when the task is high priority.
check.explanation: Contact linking describes coordination. Workspace membership remains the authentication and role system’s responsibility.

lessons.title: Prioritize tasks and review due dates
lessons.summary: Use explicit status, priority and overdue views to decide the next useful action.
lessons.prerequisites: Read earlier lessons in this path; use an authorized test workspace for exercises.

outcomes: Filter open and overdue work.
Change task state deliberately without losing the plan.
lesson.why: Dates and priorities are useful when they support decisions. Marking everything urgent hides real constraints and makes missed commitments harder to see.
preparation: Use at least two authorized test tasks or the worked example.
Choose dates according to your local calendar.

sections.heading: Understand the idea
paragraphs: Priority describes relative attention; a due date describes a commitment or review point. An overdue task is unfinished work with a valid past date. A completed task should not keep inflating the overdue count.
Status changes record human-reported progress. Moving a task to Done does not verify its linked objective. Review the objective’s measure separately.

sections.heading: Try it in BuildAndDo
steps: Edit one task to set priority and a due date.
Search for a phrase in its title or details.
Compare the All, In progress and Overdue filters.
Set an explicit task state and confirm that the saved list updates.

sections.heading: Worked example — illustrative data
paragraphs: Illustration: an overdue, high-priority consent review should be resolved before a low-priority formatting task. A task with no due date is unscheduled, not secretly overdue since 1970.

exercise.prompt: Prepare a three-item next-action list using priority, due dates and dependency judgment.
checklist: Give each priority a reason.
Exclude completed work from overdue action items.
Record a next review date for unscheduled work.

check.question: How should a missing due date be treated?
choices: As unscheduled work.
As the Unix epoch.
As automatically due today.
check.explanation: A missing value is unknown or unscheduled. Inventing a date distorts the planning view.

lessons.title: Keep useful, minimal contact records
lessons.summary: Maintain contact context without turning notes into a store for unnecessary personal data.
lessons.prerequisites: Read earlier lessons in this path; use an authorized test workspace for exercises.

outcomes: Create and edit a purpose-limited contact.
Separate notes, authority and actual outreach.
lesson.why: Useful contact records make coordination easier. Collecting more personal data than the task needs increases both confusion and exposure.
preparation: Use a consenting colleague or synthetic example.
Know why this workspace needs the record.

sections.heading: Understand the idea
paragraphs: A name, role, work email and short operational note are usually enough for a small coordination task. Do not paste credentials, identity documents or sensitive customer histories into notes.
A saved contact does not establish consent for marketing, provide account access or send a message. Any outreach needs its own authorized workflow and evidence.

sections.heading: Try it in BuildAndDo
steps: Open ERP Contacts and create a permitted test record.
Use Role to explain the person’s operational context.
Write a short note describing the reason for contact and a review point.
Edit the record to correct a detail and confirm that the saved view reflects it.

sections.heading: Worked example — illustrative data
paragraphs: Illustration: “Jordan, training coordinator, jordan@example.com; coordinates the synthetic-data workshop.” The example email is for illustration and must not be used for actual outreach.

exercise.prompt: Review a contact note and remove information that is unnecessary for its purpose.
checklist: State the reason for storing the contact.
Exclude secrets and sensitive personal detail.
Identify when the record should be reviewed or removed.

check.question: What does saving an email address do?
choices: Subscribe the person to a campaign.
Grant permission to email them.
Store a contact field; outreach and permission are separate.
check.explanation: Storage is not consent or delivery. Keep those decisions explicit.

lessons.title: Scope risk and plan recovery
lessons.summary: Write a bounded risk assessment and a rollback that preserves useful records.
lessons.prerequisites: Read earlier lessons in this path; use an authorized test workspace for exercises.

outcomes: Identify affected users, data and systems.
Define stop conditions and a recovery check.
lesson.why: Recovery is easier to design before a failure. A rollback plan should identify the state you intend to restore and the evidence you must retain.
preparation: Choose a small proposed change.
Know the environment and authority for that change.

sections.heading: Understand the idea
paragraphs: Risk depends on impact and reversibility, not only on how many lines changed. A one-line shared database change can matter more than a large local documentation update.

Rollback is not always deletion. Restoring compatible application code while retaining additive data can preserve audit history. Destructive migrations need a separate retention decision and a tested backup path.

sections.heading: Try it in BuildAndDo
steps: In a mission draft, list the systems and people the change can affect.
Describe one plausible failure and a signal that would reveal it.
Set a stop condition and name who can authorize recovery.
Write a post-recovery check that confirms the intended state.

sections.heading: Worked example — illustrative data
paragraphs: Illustration: a content preview change can be reverted while retaining drafts. Removing the collection to undo the UI change would unnecessarily destroy editorial history.

exercise.prompt: Write a four-line risk and recovery note for one ERP or content change.
checklist: Bound the environment and affected data.
Define a measurable stop condition.
Preserve records needed to understand the failure.

check.question: Which is a useful recovery check?
choices: The rollback command printed no error.
The previous accepted behavior is observed and retained data remains readable.
Someone said the system looks fine.
check.explanation: A command outcome is only one part of recovery. Verify the behavior and data you intended to restore.

lessons.title: Design four distinct TEVV checks
lessons.summary: Use testing, evaluation, verification and validation to gather different kinds of evidence.
lessons.prerequisites: Read earlier lessons in this path; use an authorized test workspace for exercises.

outcomes: Distinguish the four TEVV activities.
Connect each method to a claim and an observation.
lesson.why: A single passing test rarely answers every question about a system. Distinct checks make gaps visible before a team claims the work is successful.
preparation: Use a bounded mission with a success criterion.
Read the linked NIST guidance as context, not as a certification checklist.

sections.heading: Understand the idea
paragraphs: Testing exercises behavior under specified conditions. Evaluation assesses results against a measure or rubric. Verification checks conformance to stated requirements. Validation asks whether the result serves the intended use and users.
These categories can overlap, but copying the same assertion into four fields adds no evidence. BuildAndDo records your methods and review; it does not issue NIST certification.

sections.heading: Try it in BuildAndDo
steps: Choose one acceptance criterion in a mission.
Define an input and expected behavior for Testing.
Define a measurement for Evaluation and a requirement check for Verification.
Describe a realistic user exercise for Validation and the evidence each activity should produce.

sections.heading: Worked example — illustrative data
paragraphs: Illustration: test a draft save failure; evaluate task completion rate in a workshop; verify that approved text cannot silently change; validate that an editor can recover an interrupted review.

exercise.prompt: Create four different TEVV methods for the same small content workflow.
checklist: Name the claim each method addresses.
Specify an observable artifact.
State what remains untested or uncertain.

check.question: Which activity most directly asks whether the result serves the intended user?
choices: Validation.
Counting source files.
Checking whether a command exists.
check.explanation: Validation addresses intended use. File counts and command availability do not establish user value.

lessons.title: Apply practical OWASP checks
lessons.summary: Check authorization, input handling and data exposure at the boundary where the operation happens.
lessons.prerequisites: Read earlier lessons in this path; use an authorized test workspace for exercises.

outcomes: Identify a cross-workspace test case.
Explain why content should render as text rather than executable HTML.
lesson.why: A disabled button is helpful guidance, but it cannot protect a backend from direct requests. Security checks belong at the actual authorization boundary.
preparation: Use isolated test accounts and workspaces only.
Obtain authorization before exercising any security test.

sections.heading: Understand the idea
paragraphs: For a linked task, test that a record from another workspace cannot be selected through a direct request. Also test that a viewer cannot write and that membership removal takes effect.

For content preview, treat draft text as data. Strings that look like HTML or scripts should remain text. OWASP ASVS provides a structured verification reference; these examples are a starting point, not a complete assessment.

sections.heading: Try it in BuildAndDo
steps: Write one allowed and one denied request scenario for an ERP task link.
Include a viewer account and a removed-member scenario.
Enter harmless markup-looking text in a local draft preview.
Record the observed behavior and any test that could not be executed.

sections.heading: Worked example — illustrative data
paragraphs: Illustration: a task in workspace A must reject an objective ID from workspace B even if the browser form normally hides that choice. A server rejection is stronger evidence than a hidden option.

exercise.prompt: Add three boundary checks to a mission plan without probing any unapproved system.
checklist: Test the backend boundary, not only the UI.
Use synthetic records.
Document failed or unavailable checks honestly.

check.question: Where must a same-workspace relation be enforced?
choices: Only in the dropdown.
Only in a tutorial.
In the server request policy as well as the UI.
check.explanation: Clients can be bypassed. The server must validate the actual linked record and current caller permissions.

lessons.title: Build a workflow with an approval checkpoint
lessons.summary: Save a reusable procedure and record its ordered steps with an explicit approval decision.
lessons.prerequisites: Read earlier lessons in this path; use an authorized test workspace for exercises.

outcomes: Separate workflow activation from a recorded run.
Use an approval checkpoint before a consequential step.
lesson.why: A reusable definition makes repeat work consistent. A separate run history preserves what was actually recorded for a particular attempt.
preparation: Use an authorized test workspace with the workflow backend installed.
Have an owner or admin available for an approval exercise.

sections.heading: Understand the idea
paragraphs: Workflow definitions describe steps; runs preserve a snapshot of the definition at start. Editing a definition later should not rewrite history.

The current workflow system records operator-performed work. A notify step does not itself deliver a message. Approval checkpoints require the current owner/admin role and an explicit recorded decision.

sections.heading: Try it in BuildAndDo
steps: Create a draft workflow with read, approval and record steps.
Write a concrete expected observation for each step, then activate the saved definition.
Start a real test run and record the first outcome.
Have the authorized approver decide the checkpoint and inspect the resulting evidence receipt.

sections.heading: Worked example — illustrative data
paragraphs: Illustration: inspect a synthetic draft, approve its use in training, then record the training artifact. Activating the definition alone should not add a run or invent a last-run timestamp.

exercise.prompt: Record one approved checkpoint and inspect the run snapshot.
checklist: Keep each decision in the original step order.
Identify the saved approval actor and time.
Do not claim external tool execution from a recorded step.

check.question: What does activating a workflow prove?
choices: All its steps ran.
The definition is available to start; it does not prove an execution.
An external message was sent.
check.explanation: Definition state and execution history are separate. A real run begins with the start command.

lessons.title: Review a failed run and retry safely
lessons.summary: Preserve observations after failure and avoid creating duplicate evidence when a response is uncertain.
lessons.prerequisites: Read earlier lessons in this path; use an authorized test workspace for exercises.

outcomes: Distinguish a rejected operation from a lost response.
Explain why terminal runs are retained.
lesson.why: A failed attempt can teach as much as a passing one if the record is preserved. Retrying carelessly can turn a recoverable network problem into duplicate work.
preparation: Use a test workflow and synthetic observations.
Do not cause failures in a shared production service.

sections.heading: Understand the idea
paragraphs: A lost response does not prove that the server did nothing. The workflow client retains a request key so an identical retry can return the saved result instead of appending a second receipt.

Expected revisions protect against stale tabs. If another operator advances the run, reload its state before making a new decision. A terminal failed or cancelled run is historical; new work needs a new attempt.

sections.heading: Try it in BuildAndDo
steps: Inspect a failed test run and read its reason and recorded observations.
Compare the last accepted revision with the current step.
Use the documented retry for an uncertain response without changing the request’s meaning.
Write a reflection and a bounded next attempt instead of rewriting the failed outcome.

sections.heading: Worked example — illustrative data
paragraphs: Illustration: the server commits one evidence receipt, but the browser loses the response. Reusing the same request identity should reveal that receipt; creating a new identity may request a new operation.

exercise.prompt: Write a recovery note for a lost response and a separate note for a rejected stale decision.
checklist: Preserve the original observation.
Refresh state after a revision conflict.
Define a new attempt only when its scope is clear.

check.question: What is the first conclusion after a network response is lost?
choices: The outcome is uncertain; reconcile using the existing request identity.
Nothing was saved.
The run is verified.
check.explanation: Transport failure and business-operation failure are different. Reconcile the durable result before repeating work.

lessons.title: Write an audience-focused content brief
lessons.summary: Give a draft one reader, one useful purpose and an explicit connection to a business objective.
lessons.prerequisites: Read earlier lessons in this path; use an authorized test workspace for exercises.

outcomes: Save a draft brief in the content desk.
Separate a desired reader action from an unsupported promise.
lesson.why: A clear brief reduces rewrites because the reviewer knows whom the content serves and what the reader should be able to do afterward.
preparation: Choose a permitted topic and one audience.
Have a saved ERP objective if the draft should support it.

sections.heading: Understand the idea
paragraphs: A brief explains the reader’s situation, useful takeaway, available evidence and limits. “Everyone” is usually too broad to guide language or examples.

The content desk creates editable outlines from your brief. It does not invent research or call a private generation service. Any factual claims in the finished copy remain the author’s and reviewer’s responsibility.

sections.heading: Try it in BuildAndDo
steps: Open Community, then the Content studio tab, and choose New draft.
Select a format and name the specific intended audience.
Write the brief and a clear optional next action; link an objective if appropriate.
Save the draft and reopen it before generating or editing an outline.

sections.heading: Worked example — illustrative data
paragraphs: Illustration: “Audience: front-desk coordinators testing reminders. Takeaway: compare two templates with synthetic appointments. Next action: review the consent checklist.” No revenue or delivery guarantee is needed.

exercise.prompt: Write a brief for a short piece that helps one reader perform one task.
checklist: Name a specific reader.
Identify supporting evidence or research still needed.
Make the next action optional and clear.

check.question: Which statement belongs in a useful brief?
choices: This will double every customer’s revenue.
Write something for everybody.
Help first-time editors review a draft using a named checklist.
check.explanation: The last statement names a reader and a useful action without promising an unobserved outcome.

lessons.title: Turn a brief into a blog draft
lessons.summary: Use an outline to produce a readable article with a problem, practical steps and stated limits.
lessons.prerequisites: Read earlier lessons in this path; use an authorized test workspace for exercises.

outcomes: Generate and edit a blog outline.
Preview headings, paragraphs and lists before requesting review.
lesson.why: An outline provides structure so the writer can focus on supported content. A template should make missing evidence obvious rather than fill it with confident-sounding claims.
preparation: Have a saved or unsaved blog brief.
Gather public sources you are allowed to cite.

sections.heading: Understand the idea
paragraphs: Start with the reader’s problem, explain the useful action, then present evidence and limitations. Replace bracketed outline prompts with your own reviewed writing.
The preview supports simple headings and lists and treats text as text. Pasted HTML is not an instruction to execute. Do not confuse a formatted preview with a published page.

sections.heading: Try it in BuildAndDo
steps: Choose Blog article in a new draft and complete its audience and brief.
Use Create outline on an empty body; confirm before replacing existing copy.
Replace prompts with short paragraphs, useful steps and attributable facts.
Open Preview, inspect the structure, then save the draft before requesting review.

sections.heading: Worked example — illustrative data
paragraphs: Illustration: an article about reminder testing describes a small synthetic experiment, gives its procedure and admits that production delivery was not measured. It does not turn that experiment into a customer success story.

exercise.prompt: Produce a 150–250 word draft with one heading, one list and one explicit limitation.
checklist: Remove all outline prompts.
Attribute any factual claim that needs a source.
Check that the next action follows naturally.

check.question: What does Create outline provide?
choices: A published article.
Editable structure based on your input.
Independently verified research.
check.explanation: The outline is a writing aid. The author supplies content, evidence and review.

lessons.title: Design a tutorial people can test
lessons.summary: Write an instructional draft with preparation, observable steps, an exercise and useful feedback.
lessons.prerequisites: Read earlier lessons in this path; use an authorized test workspace for exercises.

outcomes: Define an observable learning outcome.
Write a knowledge check that diagnoses a misconception.
lesson.why: A tutorial succeeds when a learner can perform and check a task. Explanations without an exercise are difficult to test with real readers.
preparation: Choose one small task you can perform yourself.
Use examples without private customer data.

sections.heading: Understand the idea
paragraphs: State what the learner will do and what they need first. Each step should contain an action and an expected observation, with a recovery instruction where mistakes are likely.

A good knowledge check tests understanding rather than word recognition. Explain why the correct answer works and what misconception the alternatives reveal. Completion records learning activity, not professional certification.

sections.heading: Try it in BuildAndDo
steps: Select Tutorial in the content desk and describe the learner and outcome.
Create the outline and fill the preparation and ordered steps.
Add a clearly labelled worked example and a short independent exercise.
Ask a reviewer to follow the draft using only the written instructions.

sections.heading: Worked example — illustrative data
paragraphs: Illustration: a task-linking lesson asks the learner to save a task, reopen it and identify its objective. A question about whether a contact link grants access exposes an important permission misconception.

exercise.prompt: Draft a five-step lesson and one three-choice question with an answer explanation.
checklist: Make the outcome observable.
Separate illustrative values from real records.
Include a way to check and recover from an error.

check.question: Which feedback helps a learner most?
choices: An explanation connecting the answer to the underlying rule.
Wrong.
A score without context.
check.explanation: Explanatory feedback supports transfer to another task. A bare score does not explain how to improve.

lessons.title: Adapt a draft for a social post
lessons.summary: Distill one supported takeaway into a short channel-specific draft.
lessons.prerequisites: Read earlier lessons in this path; use an authorized test workspace for exercises.

outcomes: Create a social draft from a reviewed idea.
Preserve source context and one clear next action.
lesson.why: Shorter copy should preserve the meaning and limits of the source. Compression is not permission to replace uncertainty with a guarantee.
preparation: Use source material you own or have permission to adapt.
Know the audience and intended channel.

sections.heading: Understand the idea
paragraphs: Choose one useful observation, one explanation and one next action. Keep the wording understandable without requiring readers to know internal acronyms.
Channel names and planned dates in the desk are editorial metadata. They do not connect an account, send a post or prove delivery. Publishing still happens through a separately authorized process.

sections.heading: Try it in BuildAndDo
steps: Create a Social post draft and name its audience and channel.
Use the outline to write a short hook and practical takeaway.
Keep a source reference and any limitation essential to the claim.
Preview, save and request review; do not label the item published to simulate delivery.

sections.heading: Worked example — illustrative data
paragraphs: Illustration: “Our test workflow now records one receipt per accepted decision” is narrower than “Our automation never fails.” Link the actual test evidence when available.

exercise.prompt: Adapt a short blog paragraph into a social draft without adding a new claim.
checklist: Keep the original meaning.
Retain a relevant source or limitation.
Choose one optional next action.

check.question: Does setting a planned date send a social post?
choices: Yes, immediately.
Yes, through every connected channel.
No; it records an editorial plan, not an external publishing job.
check.explanation: Planning and delivery are separate. The current public content desk does not publish to external accounts.

lessons.title: Review content before approving it
lessons.summary: Check accuracy, privacy, rights and accessibility before approving a specific saved draft.
lessons.prerequisites: Read earlier lessons in this path; use an authorized test workspace for exercises.

outcomes: Record four review checks and an explanatory note.
Return changed copy to draft for a new review.
lesson.why: Review should attach to the copy someone actually inspected. Quietly changing approved text breaks the connection between the decision and its object.
preparation: Use a saved draft with audience and body.
Have a workspace owner or admin available to record approval.

sections.heading: Understand the idea
paragraphs: Accuracy asks whether claims are supported and limits are visible. Privacy checks unnecessary personal information. Rights checks permission to use the material. Accessibility checks structure and understandable language.

The server attributes approval to the authenticated reviewer and records the time. Approved copy and its brief must return to draft before editing. The checklist records a human review; it does not certify legal or technical compliance.

sections.heading: Try it in BuildAndDo
steps: Request review for a saved draft.
As an authorized reviewer, read the actual copy and its brief.
Record the four checks and explain evidence or changes in the review note.
Approve only after the checks are satisfied; otherwise return the item to draft.

sections.heading: Worked example — illustrative data
paragraphs: Illustration: a tutorial uses a customer screenshot without permission. Return it to draft and replace the image with a synthetic example before approval, rather than checking Rights without evidence.

exercise.prompt: Review a test draft and identify one useful correction before approving it.
checklist: Inspect the saved copy, not just its title.
Record why the checks passed.
Request a new review after a substantive edit.

check.question: What should happen when approved copy needs a factual correction?
choices: Edit it silently while keeping approval.
Return it to draft, correct it and request review again.
Change the publication URL only.
check.explanation: The approval applies to the reviewed content. A correction must receive a new review before publication is recorded.

lessons.title: Record a publication without inventing delivery
lessons.summary: Keep an approved draft, a planned date and an observed publication URL as distinct records.
lessons.prerequisites: Read earlier lessons in this path; use an authorized test workspace for exercises.

outcomes: Plan an approved item without claiming automatic publishing.
Record a checked HTTPS publication URL.
lesson.why: Publication history helps explain what readers could actually see. Recording a plan as a successful delivery would make later evaluation unreliable.
preparation: Use approved test content.
Publish only through an independently authorized channel and environment.

sections.heading: Understand the idea
paragraphs: A planned date is an editorial commitment. It is not an installed scheduler. The public desk sends no external posts and does not hold channel credentials.

An owner or admin can record the HTTPS URL of a publication they checked. The server records who made that assertion and when. This is an operator receipt, not an automated proof that every audience member received the content.

sections.heading: Try it in BuildAndDo
steps: Inspect the saved approval on a content item.
Optionally save a planned date and confirm the item is labelled Planned.
After an authorized publication outside this desk, open its URL and inspect the actual copy.
Use Record publication with that URL; retain the resulting history instead of editing it.

sections.heading: Worked example — illustrative data
paragraphs: Illustration: a training article is approved on Monday and planned for Tuesday. Until the operator checks the actual published page, its state remains a plan rather than a publication receipt.

exercise.prompt: Write the evidence you would require before recording a publication. Do not publish merely to complete this lesson.
checklist: Distinguish approval, plan and observed result.
Use an actual checked URL when recording a real receipt.
State the limits of the receipt.

check.question: What does the recorded publication time represent?
choices: When the server recorded the operator’s publication assertion.
Guaranteed delivery to every reader.
The exact time an external platform first published the page.
check.explanation: The timestamp belongs to the recording operation. External first-publication time requires separate evidence.

lessons.title: Run a weekly operations review
lessons.summary: Connect ERP work, mission evidence and editorial plans in a short repeatable review.
lessons.prerequisites: Read earlier lessons in this path; use an authorized test workspace for exercises.

outcomes: Review open objectives and overdue work.
Choose a bounded next action based on evidence.
lesson.why: A regular review converts scattered updates into explicit decisions. It should reduce uncertainty, not produce a decorative report full of unverified achievements.
preparation: Use the current workspace and a defined review period.
Keep business figures in their original source and currency context.

sections.heading: Understand the idea
paragraphs: Start with objective measures, then inspect tasks and related mission evidence. A completed task may be useful progress even when the objective’s target is not yet met.
Review content plans separately from actual publication receipts. Do not count scheduled items as delivered or combine unrelated financial amounts without a common basis.

sections.heading: Try it in BuildAndDo
steps: Read active ERP objectives and their success measures.
Inspect unfinished or overdue tasks and assign one clear next action to each relevant item.
Review mission outcomes and the strongest evidence from the period.
Inspect content awaiting review and planned items; record decisions in your authorized work record.

sections.heading: Worked example — illustrative data
paragraphs: Illustration: three tasks are done, one objective still lacks a baseline, and two articles await review. A useful next week begins with baseline collection and review, not an unsupported “all goals achieved” statement.

exercise.prompt: Prepare a five-line review: observed result, open question, blocker, next action and review date.
checklist: Define the review period.
Separate activity from outcome.
Keep one source with each important conclusion.

check.question: Does completing all linked tasks automatically achieve an objective?
choices: Yes, tasks are the objective.
Yes, if they were high priority.
No; assess the objective’s success measure separately.
check.explanation: Tasks are actions. The objective describes the desired result, which still needs its own observation.

lessons.title: Check a lesson on mobile and keyboard
lessons.summary: Test reading order, controls, focus and narrow layouts with observable checks.
lessons.prerequisites: Read earlier lessons in this path; use an authorized test workspace for exercises.

outcomes: Exercise keyboard navigation and focus return.
Inspect lesson structure and narrow-screen readability.
lesson.why: Content is useful only if people can reach and understand it. A desktop screenshot alone does not show whether a keyboard or small-screen reader can complete the flow.
preparation: Use a browser and a keyboard.
Choose a lesson and a test draft; avoid changing shared records without permission.

sections.heading: Understand the idea
paragraphs: Meaningful headings, labelled controls and visible focus help readers orient. Dialogs should keep focus within the open interaction and return it to the opener when closed.

Test at narrow widths and increased zoom. Look for horizontal page overflow, clipped buttons and long unbroken text. WCAG guidance supports a broader review; these checks do not replace a complete accessibility evaluation.

sections.heading: Try it in BuildAndDo
steps: Navigate to the Field Manual with Tab and open a lesson using the keyboard.
Move through controls, answer choices and the exercise confirmation.
Close the reader with Escape and check that focus returns to the lesson control.
Repeat at 320 and 375 px widths, in both themes, and note any unreadable or unreachable content.

sections.heading: Worked example — illustrative data
paragraphs: Illustration: a long title should wrap instead of pushing a completion button off-screen. A visible close icon also needs an accessible name so its purpose is available without sight.

exercise.prompt: Record one passing keyboard check and one narrow-screen observation with the viewport used.
checklist: Check focus visibility and return.
Read headings in a useful order.
Record actual observations rather than a blanket accessible claim.

check.question: Which evidence supports keyboard usability?
choices: The page uses a popular component library.
A user can reach, operate and leave the dialog using the keyboard.
The page looks good in a screenshot.
check.explanation: Observed operation is stronger evidence than the choice of library or a static image.

lessons.title: Evaluate content against its purpose
lessons.summary: Measure a draft’s or publication’s usefulness without inventing traffic, revenue or causal claims.
lessons.prerequisites: Read earlier lessons in this path; use an authorized test workspace for exercises.

outcomes: Define a small evaluation and its limits.
Record observed outcomes separately from predictions.
lesson.why: Content metrics are meaningful when they connect to the intended reader action. A large view count may say little about whether the reader could complete the task.
preparation: Choose one content brief and its intended action.
Use consenting test readers or an authorized analytics source.

sections.heading: Understand the idea
paragraphs: Before the exercise, define the audience, task, measure and observation period. In a tutorial test, task completion and the point of confusion may be more useful than likes.
Separate prediction from observed result. A change in a metric does not by itself prove that the content caused it; audience, timing and other releases may have changed too.

sections.heading: Try it in BuildAndDo
steps: Read the content brief and choose one intended reader action.
Define a small test and how you will record completion or confusion.
Collect authorized observations and retain their source and date.
Compare results with the original objective; record uncertainty and a useful next revision.

sections.heading: Worked example — illustrative data
paragraphs: Illustration: three of four consenting test readers link a task to an objective without help. Record the small sample and the step where the fourth reader hesitated; do not generalize it to every customer.

exercise.prompt: Design an evaluation note with a measure, sample, source and limitation.
checklist: Tie the measure to the reader’s task.
Label small or incomplete samples.
Avoid unsupported causal or commercial claims.

check.question: What can a four-reader workshop establish?
choices: Observed results for those readers under the recorded conditions.
Guaranteed success for all users.
Revenue impact across the business.
check.explanation: The observation is useful within its scope. Broader claims require broader evidence.

lessons.title: Verify a release from source to served version
lessons.summary: Separate source, merge, build, deployment and the version a browser actually receives.
lessons.prerequisites: Read earlier lessons in this path; use an authorized test workspace for exercises.

outcomes: Name the distinct delivery stages.
Explain how a release stamp and user-flow check support deployment acceptance.
lesson.why: A merged pull request can coexist with a failed build or an old live site. Release evidence should connect the intended source to the artifact and the observed environment.
preparation: Use public-safe release metadata from an authorized operator.
Do not change infrastructure or run deployment commands as a lesson exercise.

sections.heading: Understand the idea
paragraphs: A commit identifies source; a merge puts source on a branch. A build produces an artifact. Deployment places an artifact in an environment. A served-version check observes what that environment returns.

BuildAndDo generates version.json with its build version and commit SHA. Compare it with the accepted release receipt and inspect real behavior as well: a version file alone cannot prove every backend migration or user flow works.

sections.heading: Try it in BuildAndDo
steps: Read the source revision and test results attached to an accepted change.
Find its build and environment deployment receipt through the authorized operator.
Compare the confirmed environment’s version.json with the expected release identity.
Exercise a permitted read or test flow and record the result, timestamp and remaining gaps.

sections.heading: Worked example — illustrative data
paragraphs: Illustration: source merges successfully but the candidate job never starts. That proves a source merge, not an updated staging site. An independent private runner still needs tests, a build, deployment evidence and served checks.

exercise.prompt: Prepare a release evidence table with source, build, deployment, served version and behavior rows; mark unavailable evidence unknown.
checklist: Bind evidence to one accepted source revision.
Check staging and production separately.
Never turn a missing or skipped job into a passing result.

check.question: Does a merged pull request prove that production serves the change?
choices: Yes, merging always deploys.
Yes, if no one reported an error.
No; build, deployment and served behavior need separate evidence.
check.explanation: Delivery is a chain of observed steps. A merge establishes only the source integration step.
